title: The Brontës' tiny books
hook: The young Brontës wrote books small enough for toy soldiers to hold.
peek: As children, Charlotte, Branwell, Emily and Anne Brontë wrote whole magazines and stories in books a few centimetres tall, in handwriting so small it needs a magnifying glass. They were meant for a box of toy soldiers.
lede: In 1826 Patrick Brontë brought home a box of twelve wooden toy soldiers for his son Branwell. Each of the four children claimed one, and the soldiers became the heroes of a made-up world. The children then wrote the soldiers' books, newspapers and magazines, each one hand-sewn and small enough for a wooden soldier to read.

bullets.text: The children wrote in tiny letters made to look like printed type, packing many words onto pages a few centimetres across. The script may also have kept the stories private from adults, who could hardly read them without help.
Charlotte and Branwell built an imaginary kingdom first called Glass Town and later Angria, with its own politics, rivalries and romances. Charlotte kept writing Angrian stories into her twenties.
Emily and Anne broke away to create their own island world, Gondal. Its prose stories are lost, but many of Emily's poems were written in the voices of Gondal characters.
Charlotte made her own editions of a magazine for the soldiers, complete with stories, poems and advertisements. Single issues have since sold at auction for hundreds of thousands of pounds.
